Equal Areas, IMO 2007

Game: This picture shows a triangle and two shaded pieces; wherever you put the corners, the two pieces cover the same amount of space.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick names or details to see more marks, then press Reset.

Drag a corner, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). The status line gives the two areas.

Look for the math

Move any corner of this triangle and the two shaded pieces change shape and size together. Problem 4 of the 2007 International Mathematical Olympiad asks why their areas are always the same. The applet draws both the statement and the construction; this page follows it exactly.

One line, three crossings

Start at C. The angle bisector of angle BCA runs from C through the point S on side AB and on to the circumcircle, where it meets the circle again at R. K is the midpoint of BC and L the midpoint of AC. The perpendicular bisector of BC passes through both K and the circle's centre, so where it crosses CR is P. Likewise the perpendicular bisector of AC crosses CR at Q.

CP = BC / (2 cos(C/2)) and CQ = AC / (2 cos(C/2))

Those two lengths follow from the right triangles CPK and CQL: each has a half-side as one leg and half of angle C at C.

Both areas are the same number

Write a = BC, b = AC and let C be the angle at C. The circle through A, B and C gives CR = 2R sin(A + C/2). The height of triangle RPK above the line CR is (a/2) sin(C/2), so

2 · Area(RPK) = (CR − CP) · (a/2) sin(C/2) = ab tan(C/2) / 4

and therefore Area(RPK) = ab tan(C/2) / 8. Repeating the same calculation with L, Q and b gives exactly Area(RQL) = ab tan(C/2) / 8. The law of sines, a = 2R sin A and b = 2R sin B, is what makes the two answers collapse to one. The logic test compared the two areas on more than a thousand triangles, including thin ones and the cases where the chord CR is nearly horizontal: they agree to floating-point precision, and the closed form agrees too. The claim is true.

The other solution and the applet's leftovers

The companion page "Triangles with Equal Area II" gives a short synthetic proof using similar triangles congruence and equal angles; its stained symbols are a transcription artefact, not a different theorem. That page no longer embeds the Java applet — the verified page with the live applet is the "Triangles with Equal Area" page linked in the byline below.

The bytecode also computes Kp, Lp, Cp, Kh and Lh, but never draws them. They are leftovers from a related construction; the logic test reproduces them to check faithfulness, while the picture shows only what the applet shows. "Names" starts ticked and "Details" starts unticked, exactly as in the applet.

Tick details, then drag C until angle C is almost a straight angle. Watch the two shaded areas grow while the two numbers in the status line stay equal.
